chapter-opener@3x:
1. A Quarrel with Small Decisions
The margin is not empty space. It is where the page admits that it cannot say everything at once, and where a reader, given room, writes back. A transcription that loses the margin
loses the argument about the text as surely as one that loses a clause.
two-column@3x:
The margin is not empty space. It is where the page admits that it cannot say
everything at once, and where a reader, given room, writes back. A transcription that
loses the margin loses the argument about the text as surely as one that loses a clause.
The ratio fell from 48.2% to 40.7% between 1990 and 2019, then rose again; the sign
matters more than the level, and —-1.5% is not the same claim as 1.5%. An engine that
drops the minus has not made a small error, it has reversed a finding.

A clipboard of 2,340 tokens, a price of £1,024.50, a dose of 250 pg, a speed of 12.5
km/h: units, signs and decimals carry content, and none of them is decoration. Note
also the abbreviations that a reader must not expand, e.g. U.S. and i.e.

Some words are one keystroke apart, and the pairs are cruel: form and from, then and
than, causal and casual, affect and effect. Each survives a spell-checker, each changes
the sentence, and each is exactly the error an audit is looking for.

Emile said the café on the corner charged a naive visitor a U.S. dollar price out of a
British till, e.g. £1,024.50 for a coffee, i.e. an error no reader would forgive. Accents
and currency symbols are not decoration either.

The transformation of a page into text is a distribution of doubt across a thousand
small decisions, and each one is invisible until it is wrong. The same is true of the
distribution of a budget across a decade of commitments.

A reader that reads a column and then the other column reads a page; a reader that
reads across the gutter reads a nonsense, and the nonsense is fluent. Fluency is
exactly what makes a scrambled page hard to notice, since every sentence still ends
where a sentence can end.

Consider the two claims that differ by a comma: a dollar price in a British till, and a
dollar price, in a British till. One locates the till and the other locates the price, and a
pipeline that drops the comma has chosen a meaning on the reader's behalf.

Annotations are the page's memory of being argued with. A note number set as a
superscript, a bracketed reference set in blue and underlined, a rule that runs the
width of a table: each is a promise that something above can be checked, and each is
invisible to a reader that only sees shapes.

The last quibble is about order. Three engines that agree on every word can still
disagree about where the words go, and order is not a detail: a list of revisions read
out of sequence tells a different story than the one the page tells.
